title: Place Matters: The Significance of Place Attachments for Children's Well-Being

findings.consequent: Strong bonds with particular places
findings.quote: strong bonds with particular places endure (Hay, 1998).

findings.antecedent: Sense of belonging to a particular place
findings.consequent: Fundamental component of identity, security, and belonging
findings.quote: The sense of belonging to a particular place that this extract from a newspaper article conveys is a fundamental component of the way that most people understand who they are.

findings.consequent: Place identity, local social ties, personal meanings, linking life events to place
findings.quote: Long-term residence therefore strengthens place identity, facilitating local social ties, providing the time to invest places with personal meanings, and linking significant life events to place, although the quality and intensity of experiences are usually more important than simple duration (Tuan, 1977; Rowles, 1983).

findings.consequent: Place attachment
findings.quote: although the quality and intensity of experiences are usually more important than simple duration (Tuan, 1977; Rowles, 1983).

findings.consequent: Place attachment (as part of identity, memories, feelings, beliefs, meanings)
findings.quote: Place attachment is normally understood to be part of a person's overall identity, consisting of the memories, feelings, beliefs and meanings associated with their physical surroundings (Proshansky et al., 1983; Corbishley, 1995; Lalli, 1992).

findings.antecedent: Places imbued with personal, social, and cultural meaning
findings.consequent: Framework for personal identity construction
findings.quote: Places imbued with personal, social and cultural meaning therefore provide a framework within which personal identity is constructed (Cuba and Hummon, 1993; Hay, 1998).

findings.consequent: Significance of place attachment, belonging, security
findings.quote: In these circumstances, where the processes of modernization create risks and uncertainties for individuals, attachment to place, and the sense of belonging and security that it engenders can take on a particularly significant role in people's lives.

findings.consequent: Children's personal identity
findings.quote: Children gain their personal identity through their place attachment (Spencer and Wooley, 2000, p. 182).

findings.consequent: Positive and negative feelings in children
findings.quote: From a very young age, children develop (initially unconscious) positive and negative feelings about their everyday surroundings.

findings.antecedent: Unhappy social interactions/life events in ideal settings OR positive experiences/memories in poor environments
findings.consequent: Place attachment
findings.quote: As a consequence, ideal settings may not result in positive place attachment if they were the site of unhappy social interactions or life events, just as poor environments can do so if they are associated with positive experiences and memories.

findings.consequent: Positive cognitions in resilient individuals
findings.quote: Even when neither the physical environment nor the social context is ideal, resilient individuals are capable of transforming their experiences into positive cognitions (Proshansky et al., 1983; Newman, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Direct/repeated childhood experiences of places + social meaning
findings.consequent: Subsequent place attachment development
findings.quote: Direct and repeated experiences of places in childhood, together with the social meaning attached to them by children and others (e.g. parents, teachers and peers), tend to have the biggest influence on the subsequent development of place attachments.

findings.consequent: Home as main source of place attachment
findings.quote: Up to the age of four or five years, the home is likely to be the main source of place attachment.

findings.consequent: Understanding of geographical place, exploration of local neighbourhood
findings.quote: However, by the time they leave primary school, children will normally have developed some understanding of their geographical place in the wider world, and will also have experience of exploring parts of their local neighbourhood, either independently or in the company of adults, siblings and peers (Siegel and White, 1975; Matthews, 1992).

findings.consequent: Conscious attachment to places, identification with area, desire to live there
findings.quote: Typically, this is followed in the teenage years by a more conscious attachment to the places in which young people have grown up, evident in growing identification with the area and a desire to continue to live there into adulthood.

findings.antecedent: Perceived inclusion/acceptance in local community OR close connections through local ancestry
findings.consequent: Feelings of belonging
findings.quote: Feelings of belonging tend to be strongest amongst young people who perceive that they have been fully included and accepted within their local community, or who have close connections through local ancestry (Gould and White, 1968; Lynch, 1977; Hay, 1998; McCreanor et al., 2006).

findings.consequent: Identity and well-being in children and young people
findings.quote: Research with children and young people has repeatedly shown that place, identity and well-being are often closely connected (Rowles, 1980, 1983; Chawla, 1992; Twigger-Ross and Uzzell, 1996; Day, 2007; Green and White, 2007; Irwin et al., 2007).

findings.antecedent: Children's daily experience of living and learning in the environment
findings.consequent: Overall well-being
findings.quote: children's daily experience of living and learning in the environment around them is a critical factor in their overall well-being (Sustainable Development Commission, 2007, p. 6).

findings.consequent: Children's use of space (exploration range)
findings.quote: One of the main influences on children's use of space is their age, with many researchers noting the way that children typically progress from exploration and play close to home in the pre-school years, through widening exploration of their local environment in middle childhood, to town- or city-wide exploration during adolescence (Moore, 1986; Matthews, 1992; Chawla, 1992).

findings.consequent: Freedom to roam
findings.quote: This study, like many others (e.g. Jones et al., 2000), also noted that, with increasing age, boys tend to be given greater freedom to roam than girls.

findings.consequent: Favourite places (homes, gardens, streets, open spaces, parks, playgrounds, sports fields)
findings.quote: However, studies that have examined children's use of space indicate that favourite places for the majority of children include homes and gardens, nearby streets and associated open spaces, parks, playgrounds and sports fields (Moore, 1986; Gill and Sharps, 2004; Burke, 2005).

findings.consequent: Imaginative play
findings.quote: Several studies also emphasize the particular significance of unsupervised 'secret places' that facilitate imaginative play (Lynch, 1977; Moore, 1986; Thomas and Thompson, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Parental fears (safety, risk, sectarian violence, traffic, crime)
findings.consequent: Children's mobility, independent use of space
findings.quote: The levels of safety and risk posed by the local environment, as assessed by both parents and children, also have major influences on children's use of space (Garbarino et al., 1992; Thomas and Thompson, 2004).

findings.consequent: Independent mobility
findings.quote: Assessments of the dangers posed by traffic and crime in different locations also mean that children living in inner-city or other urban locations, where these issues are more prominent, tend to enjoy less independent mobility than their peers living in suburban or rural areas (Deakin, 2006; Morrissey and Smyth, 2002).

findings.consequent: Young people's perceptions of local area (safety, friendliness, helpfulness)
findings.quote: Other studies have revealed the way that fear of crime, or the presence of busy traffic, have negative impacts on young people's perceptions of their local area, affecting not only their views about its safety, but also about the level of friendliness and helpfulness of local people (Morrow, 2002; Mullan, 2003).

findings.antecedent: Unaccompanied journeys to school, unstructured use of local areas, independent visits to places/people
findings.consequent: Social/environmental interactions, personal/community identities, place attachments, feelings of belonging/security
findings.quote: For the majority of children in this study, unaccompanied journeys to school, together with the freedom to use local areas in a relatively unstructured way and to visit favourite places and people independently, facilitated a wide range of social and environmental interactions with people and places, contributing to their personal and community identities.

findings.consequent: Children's use of space
findings.quote: There is also a strong relationship between children's use of space and the rules and meanings that exist within particular cultures (Rappaport, 1978).

findings.antecedent: Rapid growth of home entertainment (TV, video games, computers) + fears (traffic, crime, stranger danger)
findings.consequent: Time children spend indoors
findings.quote: In combination with fears about traffic, crime and 'stranger danger', the increasing availability of such cultural artefacts has resulted in children spending more and more of their time indoors (Sustainable Development Commission, 2007).

findings.antecedent: Surveillance and regulation by public/private authorities (patrolling, prohibiting activities)
findings.consequent: Children's use of space
findings.quote: For example, public and private authorities often take steps to manage children's use of space through a combination of surveillance and regulation, which includes the employment of staff to patrol neighbourhoods and shopping centres, and the erection of signs prohibiting a range of activities such as cycling and playing ball games (Holland et al., 2007).

findings.consequent: Perception of injustice by children and young people
findings.quote: Restrictions like these are often perceived by children and young people to be unjust, especially as they typically lack effective means of challenging them (Morrow, 2002).

findings.antecedent: Being told off by neighbours for playing outside
findings.consequent: Playing outdoors
findings.quote: The great majority of children also report having been told off by neighbours for playing outside, with a third of seven to eleven-year-olds saying that this stopped them playing outdoors (Stockdale et al., 2003).

findings.antecedent: Protective discourse + growing anxieties about children's safety
findings.consequent: Children's freedom to use local environment ('shrinking world of childhood')
findings.quote: Several researchers and commentators have argued that a 'protective discourse' has developed over this period, with growing anxieties about children's safety greatly reducing their freedom to use the local environment (e.g. Scott et al., 1998; Morrow, 2002; Gill, 2008).

findings.consequent: Desire to spend more time outdoors
findings.quote: surveys also reveal that the overwhelming majority of children want to spend more time outdoors (e.g. Thomas and Thompson, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Limited availability of public open space
findings.consequent: Children's freedom to walk, cycle, or play safely
findings.quote: Restrictions on children's freedom of use of the local environment are also dependent on factors in the environment itself, including the increasingly limited availability of public open space in which children can walk, cycle or play safely in their local areas (Thomas and Thompson, 2004; Westbury, 2007).

findings.consequent: Children's health (obesity, mental health problems)
findings.quote: Although restrictions on children's freedom, which are not unique to the UK, are generally imposed in the name of protecting children from harm, there is growing evidence about the damaging effects that they may actually be having on children's health, evident, for example, in rising levels of childhood obesity and mental health problems (Gaster, 1991; Armstrong, 1993; Mental Health Foundation, 1999; Collishaw et al., 2004; Irwin et al., 2007).

findings.consequent: Mood, anger/anxiety, concentration/self-discipline (in children with conduct disorders)
findings.quote: Some of the evidence for this conclusion comes from studies examining the effects of increased access to the outdoors, which has been shown to have positive effects on mood, reducing feelings of anger and anxiety (Pretty et al., 2005), and improving the concentration and self-discipline of children with conduct disorders (Taylor et al., 2001).

findings.antecedent: Restricted use of local environment ('shrinking world of childhood')
findings.consequent: Development of children's place attachments, identity, security, and belonging
findings.quote: Less obvious, but arguably just as harmful, is the effect that the increasingly restricted use of the local environment is having on the development of children's place attachments.

findings.antecedent: Children in care (insecure attachments, major dislocations)
findings.consequent: Rootlessness, fragmented identity, diminished sense of self, increased anxiety/vulnerability to depression
findings.quote: Not only are children in care disproportionately likely to have developed insecure attachments to their primary care-givers, with negative consequences for the confidence with which they explore their surroundings and the degree to which they are able to successfully integrate experiences into their self-identity (Howe et al., 1999), but they have also experienced at least one major dislocation in their lives.

findings.consequent: Significance of place attachment
findings.quote: The real significance of place attachment is often only revealed in its absence (Brown and Perkins, 1992; Cuba and Hummon, 1993).

findings.antecedent: Government policies (Healthy Schools, Travelling to School)
findings.consequent: Children's independent use of local environment, strength of place attachments
findings.quote: However, it should be noted that neither of these programmes necessarily increases children's independent use of their local environment, which is the key ingredient in developing the strength of their place attachments and their feelings of belonging in their local communities (Engwright, 2008).

findings.antecedent: Increasing car ownership, school choice agenda, media reporting of crime
findings.consequent: Children's independent use of surroundings
findings.quote: Meanwhile, other aspects of social change and government policy, like increasing car ownership and use, and the school choice agenda (which has increased the length of home-to-school journeys in many areas, thereby reducing the likelihood that children will walk or cycle to school), coupled with the distorting effects of wall-to-wall media reporting of crimes involving children, serve to further undermine children's independent use of their surroundings.

findings.consequent: Children's independent use of local environments, place attachments
findings.quote: only the space-oriented approach specifically aims to increase children's independent use of their local environments, through the creation of what are often referred to as 'child-friendly communities' (e.g. Arnold and Cloke, 1998; Gill, 2008).

findings.consequent: Informal social activities, children's play
findings.quote: Areas where successful traffic calming or pedestrian-oriented measures like home zones have been introduced demonstrate an increase in informal social activities and children's play (British Medical Association, 1997; Pharaoh and Russell, 1989).

findings.antecedent: Regular experience of local surroundings (for children in care)
findings.consequent: 'Visible presence', sense of belonging, secure emotional attachments, resilience
findings.quote: For children of all ages looked after in care for prolonged periods of time, regular experience of being out and about in their local surroundings will also help to give them the sort of ‘visible presence' that is key to the development of a sense of belonging (Ross, 2007). They also provide the basis for potentially rich and rewarding inter-personal interactions, which help to build secure emotional attachments in the home and a sense of belonging in the community, thereby promoting children's resilience (Newman, 2004).
